title: BRICS Trade Union Forum 2026: the Hyderabad Declaration
author: Editorial Desk
summary: BMS hosted the 15th BRICS Trade Union Forum Summit from 14 to 16 July 2026.
body:
From **14 to 16 July 2026**, the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh hosted the **15th BRICS Trade Union Forum (TUF) Summit** in Hyderabad. According to BMS's report, the summit concluded on a historic note with the unanimous adoption of the **Hyderabad Declaration** for a **worker-centric global order**. This post explains what such a summit is, what the declaration asks for, and why it matters for workers in India.

## What a Trade Union Forum does

BRICS is a grouping of large emerging economies, and India holds its presidency in 2026. Alongside the meetings of governments, the BRICS process has a separate trade union track. The Trade Union Forum brings together leaders of national trade union centres from member and partner countries. They discuss common challenges, adopt a joint document and present it to the labour ministers of the grouping.

The theme in Hyderabad was "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability". Reports differ on attendance: one account spoke of more than 46 international delegates plus about 70 Indian union representatives, academics and experts, and another of 53 delegates from 13 member and partner countries and more than 60 other participants. Both agree that national trade union centres from Brazil, Russia, China and South Africa, along with India and other partner countries, were represented.

## Who took part

BMS's National President, Sunkari Mallesham, chaired the summit. B. Surendran, BMS's Organising Secretary, served as chief coordinator, and the BMS General Secretary, Surendra Kumar Pandey, conducted the proceedings. On the dais were trade union leaders from Brazil, Russia, China and South Africa, a Workers' Specialist of the ILO's Delhi office, and a retired judge of the Kerala High Court. The Union Labour Minister, Dr Mansukh Mandaviya, addressed the delegates and spoke of a human-centred approach to artificial intelligence. He cited the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, which he said manages accounts for nearly eight crore active subscribers, and the Employees' State Insurance Corporation, which he said serves more than 13.3 crore beneficiaries. The Governor of Telangana gave the valedictory address.

A delegation led by the TUF chairman also presented the workers' viewpoint at the BRICS Labour and Employment Ministers' meeting, held in Hyderabad at the same time. That is the main purpose of the forum: to make sure the workers' side is heard where decisions are prepared.

## What the Hyderabad Declaration says

According to published reports, the declaration is organised around four thrust areas: women and the future of work, universal social security, skills for the future, and human-centric technology. Its main points are as follows.

- **Social protection.** It describes social security as a universal human right. It urges BRICS governments to extend adequate, sustainable coverage to unorganised, agricultural, self-employed, migrant, platform and non-standard workers, and to allow benefits to move with a worker across borders.
- **Technology and AI.** It says artificial intelligence should not take final decisions on hiring, promotion, discipline, evaluation or dismissal without meaningful human oversight, and that workers should be able to challenge automated decisions. It also asks for data protection, digital literacy and a role for unions in the design and monitoring of such systems.
- **Platform work.** It welcomes the new International Labour Organization convention on decent work in the platform economy and urges members to bring national laws in line with it.
- **Skills.** It argues for continuous reskilling instead of one-time education, proposes a BRICS Skill Development Network and supports recognition of prior learning.
- **Women.** It addresses unequal pay, harassment, unpaid care work and digital exclusion, and encourages ratification of ILO Convention No. 190 on violence and harassment.
- **Just transition.** It asks that climate policy should not place its main burden on workers, and calls for income support and retraining alongside green investment.
- **Institutions.** It proposes a permanent mechanism for dialogue between BRICS governments and trade unions.

## The platform work convention

The ILO's International Labour Conference adopted Convention No. 193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy on 12 June 2026, in Geneva, by 406 votes to 8 with 36 abstentions, according to Human Rights Watch. It covers people who work through digital platforms, whether in person, such as delivery and taxi drivers, or online, such as data labellers. It asks governments to make sure workers are correctly classified, protects freedom of association and collective bargaining, and gives workers a right to ask for human review of serious automated decisions such as account deactivation. A convention only binds a country once the country ratifies it, so the declaration's call to align domestic laws is a request for action, not a guarantee.

In India, gig and platform work was defined in law for the first time by the Code on Social Security, which came into force with the other Labour Codes on 21 November 2025. It requires aggregators to contribute between 1 and 2 per cent of annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to such workers. How well that works will be one test of whether the Hyderabad language becomes practice.

## Why it mattered to BMS

India's presidency made BMS the host organisation for the trade union track, which gave it a platform to put forward its view of a human-centred economy. The summit also strengthened ties with trade union centres across the Global South. One observer's opinion piece in *Organiser* said the forum favoured cooperation among governments, employers and workers over confrontation; that is a viewpoint rather than a neutral finding, but it matches BMS's long-stated approach. At home, BMS is simultaneously pressing the Government to correct what it calls anti-worker provisions in two of the four Labour Codes, so the contrast between a warm international forum and a firm domestic demand is worth noting.

## An old slogan on a world stage

BMS's founder, Dattopant Thengadi, put forward the slogan *Workers unite the world*, in preference to the older "Workers of the world, unite", in the 1950s. The idea was that workers' unity should serve the world and not drive classes against each other. In Hyderabad it was heard in a setting of international cooperation, where delegations from several countries adopted a single declaration.

## What remains

A declaration is not a law or a treaty. Its force lies in follow-up: whether governments take up the proposed BRICS mechanism for dialogue with unions, whether platform workers in each country receive real protections, and whether skill networks and social security portability are put into practice. Union members can track those developments through BRICS labour ministers' communiqués and the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and compare them with what the Declaration asks.
